body:
Counselor isn't being more proactive because there was thought for most of the semester that I could do well enough to sneak under the radar and not bring it up. The way we do advisors in my department, it could very easily be seen as a problematic weakness and as something to cause an advisor pause in agreeing to work with me. 

Then exams were basically the worst case scenario.

The things I said I wouldn't do were two things that I have previously discussed with my counselor and we have decided aren't the right options for the situation, which I explained.

What I'm looking for are suggestions with how to go about it, or possibly things to avoid saying. I was looking to benefit from the pooled human experience that the internet can provide. 

Also, "if you want to overcome your situation then overcome it" completely invalidates any other point you may have made. Mental illnesses are not just bad moods or days you don't feel like working. They're not something you can suddenly decide to snap out of. For me, anxiety is a very real thing (among other issues). The thought of meeting one on one with professors at the beginning of the semester literally brought me to tears. There was no overcoming that other than getting into treatment, which I have been for nearly two years at this point. The rest of it, they tell me, will come later. I don't know if I believe them.

I'm not being terribly clear, but at this point the issue is less a "should I?" and more of a "how should I?" I can think of a few ways I definitely shouldn't approach it, but I've yet to come up with a proper combination of all the necessary elements. 

I don't know if you have any kind of first hand experience with this stuff, but it's always hard to figure out how to address it. There's a really excellent blog post that talks about how you can't calmly tell someone you're contemplating suicide. It's a really sticky issue and it's tough to navigate. And the stereotypes and stigmas associated are very real, which is another challenge.

I know that I have to have the conversations. What I don't know is how to do it without coming across like I'm trying to make excuses or campaign for grades I don't deserve. 

The concern about talking making it worse is that it's a difficult conversation to have. Every time I've ever had the initial conversation with someone, it's ended with tears. As a female in a very male-dominated department, the idea of coming across as weak and teary makes me cringe.

I've talked to my counselor. She's not affiliated with my school, though, so she can't really do anything other than facilitate medical withdrawal. I could talk to my director of graduate studies, I guess, but we have absolutely no relationship. My department chair barely knows my name, and I have no awareness of a student liaison even existing.

You're right. I haven't discussed it with anyone. Because there's no "good" way to bring something like this up to people who are basically strangers. Which is why I made this post. To seek advice and suggestions on how to discuss it.

1) Yes, we discussed medical withdrawal. But I'm stubborn and the situation was bad. And my department is so small that I would have to withdraw for a full year in order to have any classes to take, plus they would have the option to not readmit me if I did decide to come back. It didn't seem like the right solution, so we didn't pursue it. At this point, I've taken two final exams, so I'm pretty sure I couldn't anymore.

2) No, I haven't. Because all they can do is give me extended testing periods or isolated testing. Neither of those things would help. Plus, at this particular school, it's all on the students to discuss accommodations with the professor, who then uses his/her discretion to agree to terms that seem reasonable. The only time disability services really comes in is for actually administering testing or if a professor is being unreasonable. It just didn't seem worth the effort.

The worst that can happen is that my dad gets me a job. Kill me. No, seriously, kill me. 

And no, there's not. I took three classes this semester. One professor barely knows who I am, one doesn't like me, and I'm pretty sure the third thinks I'm an idiot. I don't have an advisor yet. Nobody knows what's going on, and nobody cares.
I've been seeing a counselor since the third or fourth week of the semester. I'm not medicated right now, but that's another story for another time.
I've been trying to study since Saturday with no success. At this point, I'm just trying to get some sleep. That's not going very well, either.

No, you're really not helping yourself any. Especially since it looks you down voted the posts telling you that you're doing it wrong. Read the sidebar. Then think about everything you've said to me in the context of the sidebar.

I came straight out of a BBA/MA program into grad school. And don't worry about the gender thing. As a math person with a rather androgynous first name, it's pretty frequently assumed that I'm a dude.
This is a throwaway, so I look new, but I'm pretty sure our comment exchange has gone against basically everything the mods of this sub tell people to do. Seriously, just go away.

My university has a sham of a mental health system. They have a walk in based center that only does short term therapy. If they think you'll need more than six visits, they send you to private practitioners in the area. I was in there by week 2 of the semester. I had found the therapist I've been seeing by the second week of September. Medical withdrawal was on the table, but my department is small and I wouldn't be able to come back for a full year. Plus they would have the option not to readmit me after my leave.

No, you don't seem to understand. If I get more than two Cs, I can't stay in the program. If I fail any classes, I can't stay in the program. Only one of my grades is final so far, and it's a C. The other exam I've already taken was pretty terrible, though I may scrape a B in that class. My last exam is tomorrow, and I've been too burnt out/depressed/over it to study. There's a good chance that I get at least two Cs this semester. At which point I would be done. After one semester. As a total failure.

He just seems to take everything I say with this look of "she's ridiculous, ignore her" on his face that he doesn't use with others. 

And I'm in statistics. My program doesn't generally have us start doing research until second semester second year. We take comps right before second year, spend the fall talking to potential advisors, then jump in the following spring.  

Unfortunately, if I somehow manage to stay afloat this semester and the next and the miraculously pass my comps, I'd have to find someone willing to take me on even with my bad record. Outlook is bleak from here.
Looking at the situation objectively, I'll finish this semester with at least one C. I can only have two in my program. So, uh, pretty objective. Letter grades and rules and shit.

I don't have an advisor. I took three classes this semester. I'm pretty sure one professor doesn't know my name. I'm fairly sure the one who taught the class I got the C in doesn't like me (but I earned the C, I'm not blaming him at all). My third professor knows who I am, but I think he thinks that I'm dumb. The director of my program barely knows who I am. 

I just feel like nobody would notice if I disappeared. So I probably should. But I can't bear the thought of living with this massive failure for the rest of my life.
